title: The council at the Kennedy farm

records.says: At 10 o'clock, the council was assembled. I was appointed to the Chair
After the council adjourned, the Constitution was read for the benefit of the few who had not before heard it, and the necessary oaths taken.

title: Daniel Whelan, the armory watchman, taken at the gate

records.says: To the best of my knowledge it was a quarter before eleven o'clock on Sunday night, the 16th of October.
records.label: Daniel Whelan

records.says: I came here from Kansas, and this is a slave State; I want to free all the negroes in this State; I have possession now of the United States armory, and if the citizens interfere with me, I must only burn the town and have blood.
records.label: Whelan, quoting Brown

title: John H. Allstadt and his slaves seized

records.says: There was a party of men came there on the 17th of October, at three o'clock in the morning.
records.label: John H. Allstadt

records.says: Mr. J.H. Allstadt and six of his servants were in the same manner seized about 3 a.m.

title: Phelps telegraphs from Monocacy

records.says: Express train bound east, under my charge, was stopped this morning at Harper's Ferry by armed abolitionists. They have possession of the bridge and the arms and armory of the United States.
records.label: Phelps to W. P. Smith, "Monocacy, 7.05 A. M., October 17, 1859"

records.says: At 7.05 A. M., Phelps arrived at Monocacy and telegraphed

title: The master of transportation doubts the news

records.says: Your despatch is evidently exaggerated and written under excitement. Why should our trains be stopped by Abolitionists, and how do you know they are such and that they number one hundred or more? What is their object? Let me know at once before we proceed to extremities.
records.label: W. P. Smith to Phelps, 9 a.m.

title: The B&O's president telegraphs President Buchanan

records.says: The United States Armory at Harper's Ferry is in the possession of rioters. The wires are cut west of Frederick. The officers of the mail train have been fired on and one man fatally wounded. You may rely on this.
records.label: John W. Garrett to Buchanan, "Baltimore, Oct. 17th—10.30 A. M."

records.says: At half-past ten he had telegraphed to the President of the United States, to Governor Wise, of Virginia, and to Major-General George H. Stewart

title: Phelps answers from Ellicott's Mills

records.says: My dispatch was not exaggerated, neither was it written under excitement as you suppose. I have not made it half as bad as it is.
records.label: Phelps, Ellicott's Mills, 11 a.m.

title: President Buchanan answers the railroad

records.says: Your dispatch has been received, and it shall be promptly attended to.
records.label: Buchanan to Garrett, "Washington, Oct. 17th, 1859—1.30 P. M."

title: The marines leave Washington by train

records.says: With a detachment of ninety marines, I started for Harper's Ferry that afternoon on the 3:30 train, taking with me two howitzers.
The Marines left for Harper's Ferry on the regular 3:30 train, arriving about 10 PM.

title: The troop train from Baltimore reaches Monocacy

records.says: Arrived here 8.10, moving cautiously with sixteen cars.
records.label: W. P. Smith, "Monocacy, 9.15 P. M., October 17, 1859"

title: Thomas Boerley killed

records.says: When I got on the hill, I learned that they had shot Boerley. That was probably about 7 o'clock.
records.label: Dr. John D. Starry

records.says: 7:00 am Townspeople begin firing on the raiders. Groceryman Thomas Boerly is killed by return fire.

title: William Leeman shot in the Potomac

records.says: I saw a man shot in the Potomac river on Monday, I suppose about one o'clock.
records.label: Dr. John D. Starry

records.says: the death, about one o'clock in the afternoon, of William H. Leeman
1:00 pm Raider William Leeman is killed as he attempts to escape across the Potomac River.

title: The Martinsburg company frees the prisoners in the watch-house

records.says: About three o'clock on Monday
records.label: Daniel Whelan, of his release

records.says: 3:00 pm At the Armory, militiamen free most of the hostages and force Brown and his men into the engine house.
we found in the room adjoining the engine-house some thirty or forty prisoners ... The windows were broken open by our party, and these men escaped
records.label: Capt. E. G. Alburtis

title: When the march left the Kennedy farm
basis: Anderson marched with Brown. Wikipedia's eleven is the time Lee and the Mason Report give for the seizure of the bridge, after a walk of more than two hours (National Park Service).

records.says: At eight o'clock on Sunday evening, Captain Brown said: "Men, get on your arms; we will proceed to the Ferry."
8:00 pm Brown and 18 of his men advance towards Harpers Ferry.
On Sunday night, October 16, 1859, at about 11 PM, Brown left three of his men behind as a rear-guard

title: When the raiders took the Potomac bridge
basis: Three accounts agree on half past ten, and Whelan, at the armory gate beyond the bridge, swore to a quarter to eleven; Lee was not there.

records.says: It was half-past ten when Kagi and Stevens, as advance guard, entered the Maryland bridge and made William Williams, the watchman, their prisoner.
About 10:30 p.m.
records.label: the march reaches the B&O bridge

records.says: The first active movement in the insurrection was made about a half past ten o'clock on Sunday night.
The capture of the place was effected before eleven on the 16th.
a party of insurgents, about 11 p.m. on the 16th, had seized the watchmen stationed at the armory, rifle factory, and bridge across the Potomac
between 11 and 12 o'clock at night
records.label: the Report, of the crossing

title: Who held the Potomac bridge
reading: Watson Brown and Stewart Taylor by night, as ordered; Oliver Brown, William Thompson and Dangerfield Newby by Monday morning
basis: Anderson gives Brown's orders as written; Byrne and Villard find Oliver Brown and a Black man, Newby, on the bridge on Monday. Higgins's memory of striking Oliver Brown at midnight is the one record that does not fit, and the replay does not follow it.

records.says: Captain Watson Brown and Stewart Taylor were to take positions at the Potomac bridge, and hold it till morning.
records.label: order sixth

records.says: Captains Oliver Brown and William Thompson were to execute a similar order at the Shenandoah bridge, until morning.
records.label: order seventh

records.says: he was seized by one (Oliver Brown, he afterwards learned)
records.label: the relief watchman Patrick Higgins, at midnight

records.says: answered quietly by Taylor and Watson Brown
records.label: of Higgins at the bridge

records.says: They quickly drove from it Oliver Brown and the rest of the guard
records.label: the Jefferson Guards at the bridge, about noon

records.says: I passed two armed men on the bridge -- a white man and a colored man. I think the white man was a son of Brown
records.label: Terence Byrne, between nine and ten on Monday

title: Where and when the telegraph was cut
reading: The line east cut by Cook and Tidd on the Maryland bank beside the bridge, at about 22:24; the line west on the Virginia bank above the armory, at about 23:05
basis: No source gives a time or a distance from town. The line ran along the railroad (Anderson), which on the Maryland side leaves the bridge downstream; the road the march came by meets it only at the bridge, so the east cut is placed there as the column arrives, and the west cut once the armory is taken.

records.says: That Captains Charles P. Tidd and John E. Cook walk ahead of the wagon in which Captain Brown rode to the Ferry, to tear down the telegraph wires on the Maryland side along the railroad; and to do the same on the Virginia side, after the town should be captured.
records.label: order fourth

records.says: Cook and Tidd were so busily engaged in cutting the telegraph wires along the road that they had no time to think.
The telegraph wires are cut East and West of Harper's Ferry, and this is the first station that I could send a despatch from.
records.label: Phelps, from Monocacy at 7.05 a.m.

records.says: The wires are cut between Frederick and Harper's Ferry.
records.label: Garrett to Governor Wise, 10½ a.m.

records.says: the telegraph wires are cut, no communication east.
records.label: A. Diffey, from Martinsburg via Wheeling

records.says: They cut the telegraph line twice, to prevent communication in either direction: first on the Maryland side of the bridge; slightly later on the far side of the station, preventing communication with Virginia.

title: Who went with Stevens to take hostages
reading: Stevens with Tidd, Cook, Osborne Anderson, Shields Green and Leary
basis: Anderson was one of them. Washington learned the names afterwards, and his Taylor and Meriam were at the bridge and the farm in Anderson's account.

records.says: The men selected by Col. Stevens to act under his orders during the night were Charles P. Tidd, Osborne P. Anderson, Shields Green, John E. Cook, and Sherrard Lewis Leary.
Charles P. Tidd, John E. Cook, Osborne P. Anderson, Lewis Sherrard Leary, and John A. Copeland
records.label: p. 283

records.says: The party consisted of Stevens, Cook, Tidd, Taylor, and the negro man Shields Green. There was a sixth man whom I did not see; but Cook afterwards told me his name was Meriam.
records.label: Lewis W. Washington

records.says: They then dispatched six men, under one of their party, called Captain Aaron C. Stevens
Brown detached a party under John Cook, Jr., to capture Colonel Lewis Washington

title: When Lewis W. Washington was seized at Beall-Air
basis: Washington's own testimony. The party left the armory once the town was taken, and Beall-Air is five miles out by the pike: a walk that ends nearer half past one than midnight.

records.says: They appeared at my chamber door about half past one o'clock in the morning.
records.label: Lewis W. Washington

records.says: The party took Colonel L.W. Washington from his bed about 1 a.m. on the 17th
It was at midnight that Colonel Washington was awakened by four armed men
12:00 am Enslavers Lewis Washington and John Allstadt are taken hostage

title: When the hostages reached the armory
basis: Starry and Phelps, who were awake in the town, both heard or saw the wagon at about four.

records.says: I suppose about half past three; some time before daylight on Monday morning.
records.label: Lewis W. Washington

records.says: We arrived at the Armory just about daybreak.
records.label: John Thomas Allstadt

records.says: About four o'clock I heard a wagon coming down the street
records.label: Dr. John D. Starry

records.says: at about 4 o'clock saw a wagon driven in the yard
records.label: conductor Phelps at Brown's trial

title: When the eastbound express reached the bridge
basis: The conductor's sworn time, which the Park Service also gives.

records.says: my train arrived at 1.25, bound east; saw no watchman at the bridge
records.label: Phelps at Brown's trial

records.says: arrived at Harper's Ferry at its usual hour, about half past one o'clock in the morning.
records.label: the Report

records.says: reached a point near the bridge at Harper's Ferry at 20 minutes of one o'clock this morning, when it was stopped.
records.label: the Baltimore American

records.says: The express train, in which our informant was passenger, reached Harper's Ferry about 1 o'clock this morning.
About 1:15 AM the eastbound Baltimore & Ohio express train from Wheeling

title: When Heyward Shepherd was shot
reading: About half past one, while the train was held
basis: Starry heard the shot and treated Shepherd; the conductor, Anderson and Starry all put it before the train left. Hinton, writing in 1894, alone puts it after.

records.says: about half past one o'clock, I heard a shot fired in the direction of the Baltimore and Ohio railroad bridge, the iron span of the bridge, and immediately afterwards a cry of distress
records.label: Dr. John D. Starry

records.says: as I got on the tresseling, I heard the report of a gun, and Hayward, the colored man, came running to me, and said, 'Captain, I am shot;'
records.label: Phelps at Brown's trial

records.says: He was ordered to stop by the sentinels stationed at the bridge, which he refused to do, but turned to go in an opposite direction, when he was fired upon, and received a mortal wound.
Just as the train was leaving, Cook recrossed the bridge ... Heyward Shepherd, the Hotel porter, was shot soon after.

title: When the express was let go
basis: Phelps telegraphed from Monocacy, 23 miles east, at 7.05. Leaving at half past six the train would have had to run at 41 mph; leaving at six it runs at 23, within the railroad's own limit, as the Patriot's six has it. The build fails if the express runs faster than 25 mph.

records.says: When daylight appeared we were finally permitted to pass, after being detained from half-past one o'clock to half-past six.
records.label: Phelps, from Monocacy at 7.05 a.m.

records.says: The train was delayed by the proceedings until half-past six o'clock
records.label: the Baltimore American

records.says: Capt. P.'s train left at six, having been detained five hours at the Ferry.
records.label: the Baltimore Patriot, 17 October

records.says: About five or half-past five o'clock this morning the deputation of armed insurgents approached the conductor and gave him five minutes to start his train and cross the bridge.
records.label: a passenger

records.says: At five in the morning, dawn faintly began to show. Phelps then decided to go forward.
directly after sunrise, the detained train was permitted to start for the eastward.
of passenger trains to twenty and twenty-five miles per hour
records.label: the speed limit introduced in the year to September 1859

title: When Colonel Lee arrived
reading: Sandy Hook soon after eleven; the marines in the armory yard before midnight
basis: Smith's telegram of that midnight, written where Lee arrived. Greene's times on that night run an hour ahead of every other record.

records.says: At ten o'clock in the evening he came upon a special train from Washington.
Arrived at Sandy Hook before 11, and car with Col. Lee arrived soon after.
records.label: W. P. Smith, "Harper's Ferry, October 18, 1859 ... 12 midnight"

records.says: 11:00 pm Colonel Robert E. Lee and 90 U.S. Marines arrive by train from Washington.
About twelve o'clock, Colonel Lee arrived, having under his command eighty-five marines
records.label: Col. R. W. Baylor

records.says: I did not reach the Ferry until about eleven or twelve o'clock on Monday night
records.label: Lee

title: How many marines came
basis: Greene commanded them.

records.says: I instantly replied to Mr. Walsh that we had ninety men available
eighty-five marines
records.label: Col. R. W. Baylor

records.says: 81 privates, 11 sergeants, 13 corporals, and 1 bugler
90 U.S. Marines

title: When the Jefferson Guards took the Potomac bridge
reading: Noon at the bridge, after reaching the heights at eleven
basis: Lee's eleven is their arrival on the ground, before they crossed the Potomac above the town and marched down the Maryland bank (Villard).

records.says: About 11 a.m. the volunteer companies from Virginia began to arrive, and the Jefferson Guards and volunteers from Charlestown, under Captain J.W. Rowen, I understood, were first on the ground.
It was about noon that the Jefferson Guards reached the Maryland end of the Potomac bridge.
It was about twelve o'clock in the day when we were first attacked by the troops.
At about noon, the Charlestown troops, under command of Colonel Robert W. Baylor, crossed the Susquehanna River [sic] some distance up, and marched down the Maryland side to the mouth of the bridge

title: When and where Dangerfield Newby was killed
reading: Just after noon, outside the armory gate
basis: Villard and Anderson put it after the Jefferson Guards' attack at noon, Villard as Newby ran back from the bridge; the Park Service's ten o'clock is earlier than the attack it follows.

records.says: Mr. Washington shot and instantly killed Dangerfield Newby, who, with William Thompson and Oliver Brown, had been driven off the bridge by the Jefferson Guards and was fleeing back to the armory. Newby was thus the first to die of John Brown's men
was shot through the head by a person who took aim at him from a brick store window, on the opposite side of the street
A light mulatto was shot just outside the Armory gate.
10:00 am … Dangerfield Newby is shot

title: The flags of truce
reading: Thompson taken at twenty past twelve; Watson Brown and Stevens shot at half past
basis: Villard's order: the flags went out after Brown had withdrawn into the engine house at noon.

records.says: at Brown's request, a prisoner named Cross went out with William Thompson to stop the firing, with the sole result that Thompson fell into the hands of the enemy.
Stevens fell, shot twice by George W. Chambers, a saloon-keeper, from a window in the Gait House
he was fired upon, and wounded severely. He returned to the engine house, and fought bravely after that for fully and hour and a half
records.label: of Watson Brown

records.says: 10:00 am … William Thompson is captured under a white flag
Noon Raiders Watson Brown and Aaron Stevens are shot while carrying a second flag of truce.

title: When the mayor, Fontaine Beckham, was killed
basis: Villard puts the Martinsburg company's attack just after Beckham's death, and Whelan, whom it freed, says about three.

records.says: Beckham was the last shot, about four o'clock in the evening.
records.label: Dr. John D. Starry

records.says: He was killed on the trusseling just above the hotel and near the water station; he was shot from the engine-house in the armory-yard.
records.label: George W. Chambers

records.says: Coppoc fired, but missed … But Coppoc was already firing again. This shot killed Beckham.
records.label: John Thomas Allstadt

title: When the rifle works were stormed
basis: Starry organised the attack.

records.says: I organized a party about half past two or three o'clock, and sent them over there
records.label: Dr. John D. Starry

records.says: I went to put on some dry clothes on at half past three o'clock, and that fight was then over.
records.label: Dr. John D. Starry

records.says: 2:00 pm Citizens storm the U.S. Rifle Works.

title: When Osborne Anderson and Albert Hazlett left the arsenal
basis: Anderson's own account has the marines at the engine house on Monday; Villard and the Park Service put the escape at dark.

records.says: Captain Hazlett and myself being in the Arsenal opposite, saw the charge upon the engine house with the ladder
In all probability they left their posts in the arsenal about nightfall on Monday
Raiders Albert Hazlett and Osborne Anderson, overlooked by townspeople, leave the Arsenal and escape across the Potomac River.
records.label: the entry for dark on Monday

records.says: about two o'clock in the morning
records.label: of their arrival at the schoolhouse

title: Where the schoolhouse stood
reading: On the road above Lock 34, about two kilometres from the bridge, within 1.5 km
basis: Cook passed Hardy's lock, a mile above the bridge, below the schoolhouse; the road the arms came down from the farm runs past it. No marker stands there.

records.says: deposited in a school-house about a mile from the village of Harper's Ferry, on the Maryland side.
records.label: the Report

records.says: the school-house in the mountains, three-fourths of a mile from the Ferry.
midway between Harpers Ferry and the Kennedy farm
I hurried on till I came to the lock kept by George Hardy, about a mile above the bridge
records.label: Cook's confession, going down from the schoolhouse

title: When the marines stormed the engine house and took Brown
reading: Stuart at the door at 6:58, the doors broken in at 7:02 and Brown cut down a minute later
basis: Greene's half past six is his order to pick the storming party, before the summons; the papers and the Park Service put the summons at about seven, and Washington was out by half past.

records.says: At half-past six in the morning Colonel Lee gave me orders to select a detail of twelve men for a storming party
At 6:30 AM Lee began the attack
At sunrise, when Lieutenant Stuart gave his signal
Shortly after 7 o'clock, Lieutenant E.B. Stuart … advanced to parley
7:00 am Brown refuses to surrender to Lt. J.E.B. Stuart.
about half-past seven o'clock on Tuesday morning
records.label: Lewis W. Washington, of his delivery

records.says: The whole was over in a few minutes.
the whole fight had not lasted over three minutes.
